newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE EARNS SECOND GOLD IN DRAMATIC FASHION.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-VIALBE EARNS SECOND GOLD IN DRAMATIC FASHION.

text.p: Russian Yelena Vialbe narrowly outsprinted Italian Stefania Belmondo in a dramatic finish to win her second gold medal at the Nordic skiing world championships on Monday.
Vialbe, who had already beaten Belmondo into second place to win Friday's opening 15-km freestyle race, defeated the Italian again to take the 10-km freestyle pursuit cross-country race.
But she had to wait for several minutes before officials confirmed that she had crossed the line a few centimetres ahead of her rival.
"When I saw 'photo finish' on the results board, I just prayed to God," said the 28-year-old Russian after winning her 11th world title.
Belmondo was originally told that she had been named as the winner on television. She was close to tears when Vialbe was officially declared the winner.
"It's tough, I really thought I had won," she said. "It's really disappointing to miss a gold medal that way but I must congratulate Yelena, who is such a great athlete."
Nobody could follow Vialbe and Belmondo when they escaped after completing the first of two 5-km laps of a demanding, bumpy circuit.
Russian Nina Gravilyuk came a distant third to earn her first medal in world championships.

Vialbe and Belmondo, who had started second and third respectively according to their placings in Sunday's 5-km classical style race, soon caught Russian Lyubov Yegorova, the winner of the first part of the pursuit event.
Yegorova eventually came sixth, just ahead of compatriot Larrisa Lasutina, the reigning world champion.
Belmondo led throughout the second lap with Vialbe just behind her.
The leading pair entered the stadium together and sprinted to the line side by side amid roars from an excited crowd.
The experienced Vialbe said she had thought at that moment of the rules which state that the first ski boot to cross the line determines who win.
"I just stretched my leg as far as I could," she said.
Belmondo said she had maybe chosen the wrong tactics by leading all the time on the second lap.
"Perhaps I should have let her overtake me but I felt so strong that I thought I could stay in front and win," she said.
As the Russians look almost unbeatable in Thursday's relay, Belmondo's last chance of a gold medal will come in the final women's race, the 30 km, on Saturday.
